extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and federal judges handling patent prosecution and §145 litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria for applying the prosecution-laches defense (including prejudice/intervening-rights rules) in patent cases, especially in §145 district-court actions seeking issuance of patents. Explains factors that indicate unreasonable or unexplained delay, burden allocation, and remand considerations for further fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of prosecution-laches defense in §145 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches is an equitable affirmative defense available to the Patent and Trademark Office in an action to obtain a patent under 35 U.S.C. §145.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote/support: “We hold that prosecution laches is a defense available to the Patent and Trademark Office in an action to obtain a patent under 35 U.S.C. §145.” (Opinion holds defense is available in §145 context and then analyzes its elements.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and general standard for prosecution laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches may render a patent unenforceable when it has issued only after an unreasonable and unexplained delay in prosecution that constitutes an egregious misuse of the statutory patent system under a totality of the circumstances; finding such delay includes a finding of prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: prosecution laches is an equitable affirmative defense; it “may ‘render a patent unenforceable when it has issued only after an unreasonable and unexplained delay in prosecution that constitutes an egregious misuse of the statutory patent system under a totality of the circumstances.’” (citing Cancer Research). The doctrine traces to Woodbridge and Webster Electric (early 1900s) and Symbol Techs. (Fed. Cir.). The court applies a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable and unexplained delay — six-year presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay of more than six years raises a presumption that it is unreasonable, inexcusable, and prejudicial, shifting the burden to the patentee to prove the delay was reasonable or that the defendant suffered neither economic nor evidentiary prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote/support: “In the context of laches, we have held that a delay of more than six years raises a ‘presumption that it is unreasonable, inexcusable, and prejudicial.’ Wanlass v. Gen. Elec. Co., 148 F.3d 1334, 1337 (Fed. Cir. 1998). That presumption shifts the burden to the patentee to prove that ‘either the patentee’s delay was reasonable or excusable under the circumstances or the defendant suffered neither economic nor evidentiary prejudice.’” (court explains use of presumption and burden-shifting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice requirement and intervening rights (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish prosecution laches (in the infringement context), the defendant normally must prove prejudice attributable to the patentee’s delay, which requires proving intervening rights — i.e., that the accused infringer or others invested in, worked on, or used the claimed technology during the period of delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original formulation: “Proving prejudice in that context requires proving intervening rights, i.e., ‘that either the accused infringer or others invested in, worked on, or used the claimed technology during the period of delay.’” The opinion applies and adapts this principle to §145 actions (see next entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening-rights rule adapted to §145 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of a §145 action, the PTO must generally prove intervening rights to establish prejudice; however, an unreasonable and unexplained prosecution delay of six years or more raises a presumption of prejudice (including intervening rights) and shifts the burden to the patentee to prove lack of prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the opinion: “Consistent with both Cancer Research and Wanlass, we now hold that, in the context of a §145 action, the PTO must generally prove intervening rights to establish prejudice, but an unreasonable and unexplained prosecution delay of six years or more raises a presumption of prejudice, including intervening rights. Applying these principles, we conclude that the PTO’s demonstration of an unreasonable and unexplained delay by Hyatt, which exceeds six years by any measure, shifts the burden to Hyatt to prove lack of prejudice.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear abuse of the PTO’s system can satisfy prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an applicant has committed a clear abuse of the PTO’s patent examination system (e.g., unduly increasing administrative burden, taxing the system, harming the public interest), that abuse and its effects may alone satisfy the prejudice requirement for prosecution laches in a §145 action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court language: “We further hold that, where a patent applicant has committed a clear abuse of the PTO’s patent examination system, the applicant’s abuse and its effects meet the prejudice requirement of prosecution laches.” Examples given include creation of an art unit, millions in extra examiner expense, impossibility of processing applications using normal procedures, and other system-wide burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific factual conduct factors evidencing unreasonable/unexplained delay or abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated prosecution behaviors that indicate unreasonable or unexplained delay or constitute abuse of the patent system: (i) presenting claims many years or decades after their priority dates; (ii) bulk-filing many photocopied applications; (iii) failing to demarcate/divide applications as instructed; (iv) dramatically increasing/unduly multiplying claims (contrary to 37 C.F.R. 1.75(b)); (v) rewriting/shifting claims in large part or entirety (contrary to 37 C.F.R. §1.145); (vi) presenting numerous duplicate or patentably indistinct claims across applications without informing the PTO (contrary to MPEP §§2001.06(b), 2004(9)); (vii) failing to identify written-description support for claims (contrary to MPEP §§714.02, 2163.06); (viii) re‑filing claims previously lost in interference proceedings; (ix) failing to take allowed claims but refiling them years later; (x) failing to prosecute §145 actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion repeatedly cites these specific practices (and cites the CFR and MPEP provisions) as evidence of abusive or unexplainable delay in Hyatt’s prosecution. The court treats these factors cumulatively under the totality-of-the-circumstances test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof allocation on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the PTO proves an unreasonable and unexplained delay (especially where it exceeds six years) or shows clear abuse, the burden shifts to the patentee to show by a preponderance of the evidence a legitimate, affirmative reason that (a) explains the delay and (b) justifies the prosecution approach and the failure to follow instructions (e.g., to demarcate applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance: “Hyatt must show by preponderance of evidence that Hyatt had a legitimate, affirmative reason for his delay. Such a reason must operate to excuse Hyatt from responsibility for the sizable undue administrative burden that his applications have placed on the PTO... Any satisfactory reason must, at a minimum, justify Hyatt’s decision to ignore Director Godici’s instruction to demarcate his applications in 1995; justify his decision to adopt the specific prosecution approach that he did… and justify his failure to develop a plan for demarcating his applications over at least the 20 year period from 1995 to 2015.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence demonstrating prejudice / concrete metrics PTO may use
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of factual evidence the PTO can rely on to prove prejudice or system abuse: creation of a dedicated art unit; disproportionate examiner-time per office action (months vs. days); number of office actions per application compared to norm; total examiner-time estimate to process applicant’s portfolio (e.g., hundreds of years); monetary disparity between examiner costs and applicant fees; combinatorial comparisons to identify double-patenting (billions of claim comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court relied on PTO figures: e.g., PTO created an art unit, spent ~ $10 million examining Hyatt’s claims while Hyatt paid ~$7 million in fees, average office action for Hyatt took ~4 months vs typical 2–3 days, estimate of 532 years of examiner time, etc. The opinion treats such metrics as probative of prejudice and system burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/evidentiary rules specific to §145 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A §145 action is a hybrid process: the applicant may present new evidence in the district court; when new evidence is presented the district court reviews de novo those issues, whereas if no new evidence is presented the court reviews the agency action on the administrative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the opinion: “The §145 action is a hybrid action... It is unlike an appeal because the plaintiff can present new evidence... However, if the applicant presents no new evidence, then the district court reviews the action on the administrative record, and the district court reviews de novo any issue for which the applicant presents new evidence.” This affects what evidence the patentee may introduce on remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review on appeal and Rule 52(c) context
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate standards: district court factual findings reviewed for clear error; legal conclusions reviewed de novo; the district court’s determination of prosecution laches is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Rule 52(c) may be used for judgment on partial findings in nonjury trials when a party has been fully heard on an issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From opinion: “We review the district court’s factual findings for clear error and its legal conclusions de novo... We review a district court’s determination of prosecution laches for abuse of discretion... Rule 52(c) provides that, in a nonjury trial, if a party has been fully heard on an issue and the court finds against the party on that issue, ‘the court may enter judgment against the party on a claim or defense that... can be maintained or defeated only with a favorable finding on that issue.’” The court vacated a Rule 52(c) judgment and remanded for further proceedings.
